newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: PRESS DIGEST - Ireland - February 11.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Ireland - February 11.

text.p: Following are the highlights of stories reported in the Irish press on Tuesday.
- The government is moving quickly to address the issue of early retirement for nurses in an effort to ensure that they vote in favour of the latest 80 million Irish pound package on offer.
- Gale force winds gusting at up to 80 m.p.h, heavy rain and sleet showers hit many parts of Ireland on Monday with serious flooding in Galway, Limerick, Tralee, Kinvara and Westport.
- The Irish Tourist Board on Monday started its most aggressive and expensive campaign ever on the Irish home holiday market.
- The office of the British Prime Minister has confirmed that it received a fax on Monday from Sinn Fein president, Gerry Adams, requesting talks.
- The currency markets have remained quiet showing virtually no reaction to weekend suggestions that the dollar has now risen far enough.
- A couple arrested on Monday in West Cork in connection with the murder of Frenchwoman Sophie Toscan Du Plantier, were released without charge on Monday night.
- An increase in public hospital charges is being considered by the Irish government to fund the extra 35 million Irish pound needed to settle the nurses dispute.
- A "sophisticated" operation for growing, harvesting and drying of cannabis plants was discovered by Irish police in West Cork.
- Ryanair, the low fares airline is planning to go public, according to market sources.
- The Irish government is expected to order spending cuts across all departments to cover the extra 35 million Irish pounds the Labour Court has recommended for nurses.
- The first shots were fired on Monday in a betting battle between bookmakers and the national Lottery.
- The rate of death on Irish roads is almost double that of the United Kingdom, a new study revealed on Monday night.
- Beef is still the country's favourite meat despite repeated scares over BSE and illegal growth promoters, according to a major survey of urban attitudes to farming and food.

- A significant number of Ireland's small haulage firms, dependant on the troubled Bell Lines freight transport group, will go out of business over the next few days if immediate action is not taken to ease their cash problems.
